footprint_note: court plus run-off, benches and officials
apex_note: peak of a lob pass or high jump shot
earth_reference: FIBA mandates 7 m of clearance over a court — exactly what this model returns at 1 g.
primary_constraint: The cheapest of the Big Five to enclose, by more than two orders of magnitude. Nothing in the game goes high and nothing in it goes far: a 4.5 m ball apex over a 620 m² footprint. Low gravity still multiplies the ceiling, but it multiplies the smallest ceiling and the smallest floor in the set.
adaptation: Raised rim assemblies and a pass-heavy game, since a 2.5 s bounce cycle kills the dribble drive long before the roof becomes the problem.

footprint_note: sheet plus boards, benches and box
apex_note: peak of a flipped clearing puck
earth_reference: Rinks are built to roughly 8 m of clearance, which this model reproduces.
primary_constraint: The second cheapest, and the only other one that stays buildable off Earth. A flipped puck is the tallest thing in the game and the sheet is small. On an ice moon the surface is already there — the enclosure is the entire cost.
adaptation: Ballasted skates and powered edge-grip blades, because at low gravity the blade cannot bite hard enough to turn or stop.

apex_note: peak of a punt with 5 s hang time
earth_reference: Real domes run 46–82 m because a roof spanning 150 m has structural depth of its own; 35 m is the ballistic floor, not a buildable roof.
primary_constraint: The punt is what breaks it. A kicking game that sends the ball 30 m up on Earth sends it six times higher on the Moon, and it is being roofed over a footprint ten times a basketball court's. Volume is the product of both, so it compounds.
adaptation: Ban or cap the kicking game and the ceiling collapses to the height of a thrown pass — the single highest-leverage rule change available to any of the Big Five.

footprint_note: pitch plus technical areas and run-off
earth_reference: Full-size indoor pitches are roofed at about 30 m, close to this model's 28 m.
primary_constraint: The largest footprint in the Big Five, paired with a goal kick that clears 25 m. Under a dense atmosphere the ball also stalls and drifts rather than falling cleanly, so the enclosure has to be wider than the pitch as well as taller.
adaptation: Weighted low-rebound balls and perimeter netting, trading the long ball for a ground game the roof can afford.

surface_note: fair and foul territory of a typical MLB field
footprint_note: field plus warning track, backstop and stands edge
apex_note: peak of a deep fly ball or high pop-up
earth_reference: Tropicana Field peaks near 68 m; 43 m is the ballistic floor.
primary_constraint: The worst case in the set, and not close. Baseball combines the largest footprint with the highest routine ball flight, and volume multiplies the two. Off Earth it is the one sport of the Big Five that is not merely expensive to enclose but arguably unbuildable.
adaptation: Nothing at the margins fixes it. Either the roof goes away — an unpressurized surface game in suits — or the sport moves indoors as a zero-g variant played to sensor rings, which is a different game wearing the same name.
